title: How Much Caffeine Is in Matcha? (Per Tsp, Gram & Latte)
h1: How much caffeine is in matcha?
meta_description: A standard 1 tsp (2 g) serving of matcha has about 65–70 mg of caffeine. See matcha vs coffee, green tea, and latte amounts — with a calculator.

body_html:
A standard serving of matcha — 1 teaspoon (about 2 grams) whisked into 2–3 oz of water — contains roughly 65–70 mg of caffeine. Depending on grade and how much powder you use, a serving ranges from about 60 to 80 mg. That's more than a cup of steeped green tea (~35 mg) but less than an 8 oz coffee (~95 mg).

Matcha caffeine by serving size

Caffeine scales directly with how much matcha powder goes into the bowl or cup. The three servings below cover the range you'll actually run into — a thin usucha bowl, a standard scoop, and a café-strength latte:

ServingMatcha powderCaffeine
Thin (1/2 tsp)~1 g~35 mg
Standard (1 tsp)2 g~65–70 mg
Strong latte (2 tsp)4 g~130 mg

Cafés vary a lot here — some use closer to 1 tsp for a latte, others go as high as 2.5 tsp. If caffeine matters to you, it's worth asking how much powder goes into the drink.

Matcha vs coffee, green tea, and espresso

Use the calculator above to compare any drink by the cup or across a full day, or check the static reference table below — the same figures the calculator uses:

DrinkServingTypical caffeineRange
Matcha1 tsp (2 g) whisked in 2–3 oz~65–70 mg60–80 mg
Matcha latte2 tsp (4 g)~130 mg120–160 mg
Green tea (steeped)8 oz~35 mg30–50 mg
Black tea (steeped)8 oz~50 mg40–70 mg
Espresso1 oz shot~63 mg60–80 mg
Brewed coffee8 oz~95 mg80–100 mg

Two things stand out. First, matcha and espresso land in almost the same range per serving — a whisked bowl of matcha is closer to a shot of espresso than to a cup of steeped tea. Second, a matcha latte's 2 tsp pour puts it closer to a small brewed coffee than to a single serving of matcha.

Why matcha caffeine numbers vary online

Search around and you'll find matcha caffeine figures ranging from under 20 mg to well over 100 mg for what's described as a single serving. The gap usually comes down to what's being measured, not a real disagreement about the tea. Some sources report caffeine per gram of dry powder; others report it per prepared cup, which depends entirely on how much water or milk the powder is whisked or steamed into. Some quote a 1/2 tsp thin-tea pour; others quote a 2 tsp latte-strength scoop. Agricultural products like tea also naturally produce a range rather than one fixed number, since caffeine content shifts with growing conditions, harvest timing, and how finely the leaf is ground.

This page standardizes on one convention throughout: caffeine per teaspoon of matcha powder used, cross-checked against the published tea-caffeine sources cited below. The comparator tool above and every table on this page pull from that same dataset, so the numbers won't drift depending on which section you're reading.

Matcha, caffeine, and L-theanine

Matcha is whole, stone-ground tea leaf, so a serving also carries a meaningfully higher dose of L-theanine — an amino acid concentrated in tea — than the same amount of caffeine delivers on its own. Published research has looked at how L-theanine and caffeine together affect measures of attention. Kelly and colleagues (2008, Journal of Nutrition) reported that the combination of L-theanine and caffeine was associated with changes in alpha-band brain activity and attention-task performance compared with either compound alone. That's a description of what the study measured, not a promise about how any individual cup will make you feel — responses to caffeine and L-theanine vary by person, tolerance, and how much you drink.

How to control your matcha caffeine

If you want to land at a specific caffeine level, the lever is powder-to-water ratio, not the tea itself:

  • Usucha (thin tea): about 2 g (1 tsp) of matcha whisked into roughly 2 oz (60 ml) of water — the everyday bowl, and the baseline for the ~65–70 mg figure above.
  • Koicha (thick tea): about 4 g of matcha whisked into roughly 1 oz (30 ml) of water — double the powder in less water, so roughly double the caffeine per serving.
  • Grade: ceremonial and culinary grades come from the same shade-grown leaf; caffeine differences between grades are small relative to the effect of how much powder you scoop.
  • Measuring tool: a bamboo chashaku scoop, a measuring spoon, and a kitchen scale can each land on a different actual gram weight for "1 tsp" of matcha, since sifted powder is less dense than packed powder. A scale is the most repeatable way to hit a target dose.

See our full breakdown of matcha-to-water ratio for gram-by-gram measurements across usucha, koicha, and lattes.

Matcha caffeine in recipes

Once matcha moves from a bowl into a latte, smoothie, or baked good, the caffeine math is still just the powder amount: matcha itself doesn't gain or lose caffeine when it's mixed with milk, blended with fruit, or baked into batter. A few common formats, using the same 1 tsp (2 g) ≈ 65–70 mg reference:

  • Iced or hot latte: most recipes and café pours use 1–2 tsp of matcha per drink, so figure roughly 65–130 mg depending on how strong it's made.
  • Smoothie: a typical home recipe calling for 1 tsp of matcha adds about the same ~65–70 mg found in a bowl of usucha, spread across a larger volume of liquid.
  • Baked goods (cookies, muffins, mochi): a batch made with 1–2 tsp of matcha divides that total caffeine across however many servings the recipe yields, so caffeine per slice or cookie is usually well under a full-serving dose.

Is matcha too much caffeine?

For most adults, a single 1 tsp serving of matcha (~65–70 mg) or even a 2 tsp latte (~130 mg) is a modest share of the general daily reference published for healthy adults — the U.S. FDA has cited about 400 mg per day as a level not generally associated with dangerous, negative effects for most healthy adults. That reference covers total caffeine intake across everything you drink in a day, not any single cup, so it's worth counting coffee, tea, and other caffeinated drinks together rather than matcha in isolation. People who are pregnant, caffeine-sensitive, or managing a health condition should talk to a healthcare provider about what caffeine level is appropriate for them.

For more on matcha itself — how it's grown, graded, and prepared — see our complete matcha guide. To see how matcha stacks up against steeped green tea beyond caffeine, see matcha vs green tea.

This describes published research and general information, not medical or dietary advice.

faqs.q: Is matcha higher in caffeine than coffee?
faqs.a: No. A 1 tsp (2 g) serving of matcha has about 65–70 mg of caffeine; an 8 oz brewed coffee has about 95 mg. Matcha has more than steeped green tea but less than brewed coffee.

faqs.q: How much caffeine is in a matcha latte?
faqs.a: Most cafés use about 2 tsp (4 g) of matcha, so a latte typically has around 130 mg of caffeine (roughly 120–160 mg), similar to a small coffee.

faqs.q: Is 2 tsp of matcha a lot of caffeine?
faqs.a: Two teaspoons (~4 g) is around 130 mg — roughly one strong cup of coffee. Published guidance puts a general adult reference at about 400 mg/day.

faqs.q: How much caffeine is in matcha per gram?
faqs.a: A 2 g serving typically lands around 65–70 mg, with a usual range of 60–80 mg depending on grade and how much powder you use — roughly 30–40 mg per gram.

faqs.q: Does matcha give jitters like coffee?
faqs.a: Matcha pairs caffeine with L-theanine. Research (Kelly et al., 2008) describes L-theanine plus caffeine affecting attention differently than caffeine alone; this is research description, not a promised effect.
